19 The OpenAI-compatible surface, and what vLLM adds

vLLM serves an OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions. That compatibility is the reason the client in vllm.rs is forty lines and the reason the model can be swapped without touching Rust. It is also a trap, because the compatible subset is not the interesting part.

FieldCompatibleNotes
model, messagesYes—
temperature, max_tokensYesChapters 20–21
response_format: json_objectYesGuarantees valid JSON, not your JSON
guided_json / response_format: json_schemavLLMGuarantees the schema. Chapter 22
guided_choice, guided_regex, guided_grammarvLLMCheaper constraints for narrower outputs
logprobsYesThe only honest confidence signal. Chapter 23
streamYesChapter 27

The URL, and a small thing done right

LLM_URL is configured as the base ending in /v1, the way the OpenAI-compatible world writes it, and completions_url() appends the path once at startup rather than baking it into the environment where every deployment would have to repeat it correctly. It tolerates a trailing slash, and there are two tests for that.

This is worth noticing because it is the pattern for every future setting: the environment carries the thing a human knows, the code derives the thing the machine needs. A .env full of full endpoint paths is a .env where one of them is wrong.

The API key, and why it is optional

vLLM only checks a bearer token when started with --api-key. Sending one it does not expect is harmless; sending none when it does expect one is a 401. So the header follows the configuration, which is the correct asymmetry.

20 Temperature, and where zero is wrong

temperature = 0.0 is correct for what this endpoint does today, and the settings file states the reason in four words: deterministic routing. The same sentence has to land on the same function every time, or the classification is not a classification.

Two things follow that are easy to get wrong.

Zero is not actually deterministic

Greedy decoding is deterministic given identical batch composition. Under continuous batching, floating-point reduction order varies with what else is in the batch, and identical requests can produce different tokens. It is rare, and it is not a bug you can fix from the client.

The practical consequence is for testing, not production: a test that asserts an exact generated sentence is flaky by construction. Assert on the structured fields — which function was selected, whether a flag is set — and never on the prose.

The phrasing wants variety, and shares the setting

Here is the tension that arrives with multi-step forms. One schema produces two kinds of output through one sampling configuration:

KeyWantsBecause
selected_function, slot values, flagsTemperature 0The same input must route the same way, every time
humanlike_sentence_answerTemperature > 0The third re-prompt must not be word-for-word the first

Three ways out, in increasing order of cost:

  1. Leave it at zero and get variety from the prompt. Layer 4 carries an explicit instruction to vary phrasing on retries, plus two or three differently-shaped sample sentences. Cheapest, usually sufficient, and the approach the realtime-prompting guidance recommends anyway.
  2. Two calls. A cold, constrained extraction call and a warm phrasing call. Clean, and it doubles the number of GPU round trips per turn, which Chapter 3 says you cannot afford.
  3. Deterministic sentence selection. The model picks a phrase key; code selects wording from a table, rotating on the attempt counter. This is how ai_autocalls_rust works — messages/phrase.rs holds every sentence, named, in every language — and it gives perfect control and perfect reproducibility at the cost of the naturalness the model was brought in for.

Option 1 until an evaluation says otherwise.

21 Bounding generation

max_tokens is the setting whose absence caused the incident recorded in context.md, and the chapter is mostly about how to choose it again after the schema changes — because it will.

What happened

Generation was unbounded, so it could run to the end of the 4096-token context window. A repetition loop on one turn therefore held the GPU for minutes. The client's 30-second budget expired first, reqwest reported it with the same Display text it uses for a refused connection, and the caller got a 502 that said “upstream is broken” about an upstream that was merely busy.

Three separate faults, one symptom. The fix was three changes, and all three are load-bearing: a token cap, a timeout sized for the bad case, and a distinct error variant (Chapter 25).

The derivation

The current numbers: the schema has eight keys and a well-formed answer runs about 100 tokens. The cap is 256, which settings.toml describes as room for a long sentence while stopping a repetition loop.

cap = ceil(p95_observed_tokens * 2.5)

The multiplier is a judgement, not a law: it wants to be large enough that a legitimately long answer is never truncated, and small enough that a degenerate generation is cut off in well under a second of GPU time. 2.5× on a ~100-token answer gives 256, which is where the current value comes from.

Rule

Re-derive the cap whenever a key is added to the schema, and record the measurement next to the value. Every key costs generated tokens; eight keys cost about 100. A form-filling schema that emits the shared contract keys plus a step's slots will not fit in 256, and the failure mode is a truncated answer, not an error at the point of the change.

In this repo

prompts/README.md already warns about this — “past the cap a turn fails with a message naming that setting, rather than a confusing parse error” — and VllmError::Truncated carries the cap in its message so the person reading the log is told which value to change. That is the standard to hold every other setting to.

Generating fewer tokens in the first place

The cap bounds the worst case. Reducing the typical case is the latency work, and it is mostly schema design:

  • Every key is generated serially. A key nobody reads is pure latency.
  • Booleans and enums are one or two tokens. Free-text keys are not; a reasoning or notes key can cost more than everything else combined.
  • Long key names are generated too. humanlike_sentence_answer is seven tokens of pure overhead on every single turn — not enough to change on its own, but worth knowing before adding requires_clarification_question as a second one.

22 Constrained decoding

The client sends response_format: {"type": "json_object"}, and the doc comment says this is what makes parsing the content below safe enough to do directly. That is true and it is worth being precise about what it guarantees, because the guarantee is narrower than it sounds.

Three levels

ModeGuaranteesDoes not guarantee
Nothing Nothing Everything. Markdown fences, an apology, a trailing comma
json_object (current) Syntactically valid JSON. It will parse Which keys. Which types. That selected_function names a real function
guided_json / JSON Schema Valid JSON conforming to your schema: keys present, types right, enums respected That the values are correct — only that they are well-formed

The gap between rows two and three is where the interesting failures live. Under json_object, the model is told the schema in prose and asked nicely. It complies almost always. “Almost always” over thousands of calls is a steady trickle of turns where a key is missing, a float arrives as a string, or selected_function is a plausible function that does not exist.

Under a schema, those are not rare — they are impossible. The decoder masks tokens that would violate the grammar, so the output cannot leave the schema whatever the model intended, which is also the injection control noted in Chapter 17.

The backends, and the cost

vLLM picks a backend automatically; the notable one is XGrammar, which classifies tokens into context-dependent and context-independent categories to cut mask-creation time, and uses pushdown automata for context-free grammars. Comparisons find it benefits substantially from caching compiled grammars.

That is the operational point: grammar compilation is per distinct schema, and it is cached. A handful of stable schemas — one per step — compile once and are reused. A schema assembled fresh per turn with keys in varying order is a new grammar every time, and pays compilation on every request.

Rule

Schemas must be stable and few. Render them from the manifest (Chapter 16) with a deterministic key order, so the set of distinct grammars in the system equals the number of steps, not the number of turns.

Measure this

The JSON-validity rate and the schema-conformance rate, separately. Today only the first is observable, as the ratio of VllmError::Malformed to successful turns. The second — how often a syntactically valid answer is missing a key or has a value outside its enum — is currently invisible, because serde accepts anything into the flattened map. Measure it before deciding whether guided_json is worth the migration; if it is already near zero, the current mode is fine and the argument is only about injection.

The narrower constraints

A full JSON schema is not always the right tool. guided_choice constrains output to exactly one of a list, which is what pure routing is, and is dramatically cheaper than a grammar. If the architecture ever splits into a fast routing call and a slower extraction call, the routing half wants guided_choice over the function names and nothing else.

23 Confidence is not calibrated

The schema asks for "confidence": float, and the model obligingly returns 0.95. That number means considerably less than it appears to.

What is wrong with it

Self-reported confidence from an instruction-tuned model is unreliable in two documented, specific ways. It is bimodal: scores cluster at 0.95+ or 0.05−, skipping the middle range that a threshold would need. And it is class-dependent: the same 0.7 represents different actual accuracies for different classes, so one threshold cannot serve them all.

A model that says it is 95% sure may be wrong 30% of the time. The number is generated text that looks like a probability.

What to use instead

Token logprobs
Request logprobs and read the probability of the tokens that spell the chosen function name. Still not calibrated — a 0.7 logprob does not mean 70% accuracy — but it is a real measurement of the model's state rather than a generated assertion about it, and it moves monotonically with correctness, which a threshold can work with.
Thresholds fitted per class
Set them from measurement, per intent, against cost. An irreversible action wants a high-precision floor — the score at which empirical accuracy clears 0.95 on held-out calls. A read-only lookup can be far more permissive. One global threshold is the thing to avoid.
Recalibration as a recurring job
Thresholds drift with every model or prompt change. Collect routing outcomes, compute a reliability diagram, and recalibrate when expected calibration error exceeds tolerance. This only works if outcomes are recorded, which is Part VII's job.
Rule

Treat a threshold as a fitted parameter, not a constant. It is valid for one (model, prompt, schema) triple and is invalidated by a change to any of them — including a prompt edit made through the hot-reload path, which leaves no deployment record. This is a second reason for the prompt hash in Chapter 18.

In this repo

confidence currently drives nothing — it is a badge in the mimic client and a field in a log line. That is the right place for an uncalibrated number, and it should stay there until it is measured. The moment it gates a branch it has moved from the flattened map to the manifest (Chapter 16), and it needs the calibration work first.

24 One GPU, many callers

A phone line is not a chat window. Turns arrive when callers finish talking, which means arrivals are bursty and every one of them is latency-critical because somebody is holding a handset.

The queueing reality

vLLM batches continuously: requests join the running batch as capacity allows. Under load the wait is not compute, it is queueing, and queueing shows up entirely in the tail. This is why the guidance throughout this book is to watch p95 rather than the mean — the mean is dominated by the quiet periods that nobody complains about.

Two properties of this workload make it better-behaved than most:

  • Output is short and capped (Chapter 21), so no request occupies the batch for long.
  • Prompts share a long prefix (Chapter 26), so concurrent callers are cheap to co-locate.

And one that makes it worse: a stalled turn is a silent phone line, so the cost of a tail event is not a slow page, it is a caller who starts talking over the agent.

Model and quantisation

The configured model is Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-AWQ — a 4-bit activation-aware weight quantisation of a 7B instruct model. For a classification-and-phrasing workload with a constrained output schema, this is a sensible point on the curve: the schema does most of the structural work, so model capacity is spent on understanding rather than on format compliance.

Measure this

Quality at the schema level, before reaching for a larger model. The tempting response to a misrouted call is a bigger model. The cheaper interventions, in order: fix the capability description (Chapter 14), constrain the output (Chapter 22), add one canonical example. A scenario suite (Chapter 38) is what tells you which one worked, and without it the model swap is a guess that costs VRAM.

Trap

The context window is 4096 tokens. Nothing in the current design comes close — but layer 5 rendering, a turn window, a form manifest and a per-step schema all add prefix, and a long-running call with an unbounded window is exactly how a system discovers its context limit: mid-call, on the longest and most invested conversation of the day. Bound the window (Chapter 15) and assert the assembled length at load time.

25 A failure taxonomy that names its own cause

This chapter is short because the project already got it right, and the value is in stating the principle so it survives the next refactor.

The original failure

The first 502 this endpoint produced logged error sending request for url (...), which is all reqwest's Display prints. It hides the cause: a 30-second timeout and a refused connection read identically. Somebody looking at that line cannot tell whether the GPU container is down or merely slow, and those have opposite responses.

The taxonomy

VariantHTTPMeansFix
Timeout { budget_seconds }504 Slow or contended inference server Retryable. Investigate load, not health
Transport502 Genuinely broken upstream Check the container, the URL, the network
NoChoices502 Well-formed response with nothing in it Server-side; rare; worth alerting
Truncated { max_tokens }502 Our own cap cut the answer off Raise llm_settings.max_tokens — named in the message
Malformed { source }502 The model emitted something that is not the schema Prompt or decoding mode (Chapter 22)

The Truncated / Malformed split is the one worth studying. Both present identically — a string that will not parse — and they have opposite causes: one is a configuration value set too low, the other is a model or prompt problem. finish_reason == "length" is the only thing that distinguishes them, which is why Choice deserialises a field it otherwise has no use for, with a test asserting it survives.

Rule

One error variant per distinct operator response, not per distinct code path. Two failures that lead to the same action can share a variant; two failures that lead to different actions must not, however similar their symptom. The test is: could someone reading only the log line pick the right next step?

What to add as the system grows

  • SchemaViolation — conformed to JSON, not to the manifest. Distinct from Malformed once guided_json is in use.
  • SlotRejected — parsed, but the validator said no. Not an error at all: it is a conversational turn (Chapter 8) and must not become a 502.
  • PromptAssembly — a template referenced a variable that does not exist. Should be impossible after Chapter 18's load-time validation, which is a reason to have the variant: if it ever fires, the load-time check has a hole.

26 Prefix caching, and what breaks it

vLLM keeps KV blocks in a hash table keyed by the token sequence from the start of the request, so a request sharing a prefix with an earlier one reuses that computation. For chat workloads with long shared system prompts the reported saving is 60–80% of time-to-first-token.

Given Chapter 3's arithmetic — the model stage is the largest item in a budget this service is already over — that is the single largest latency lever available without changing hardware or architecture.

The mechanics that matter

  • Blocks are 16 tokens, and only complete blocks are cached. A prefix ending mid-block earns nothing for that block.
  • The key is the whole sequence from position zero. One differing token near the front invalidates everything after it. There is no partial credit for a prompt that matches in the middle.
  • Blocks are evicted. A prompt used once an hour will not be resident. Few, stable, frequently-used prefixes beat many rarely-used ones.
  • There is overhead when the hit rate is near zero — hashing and table comparison are not free. A workload with no shared prefixes is slightly worse off with caching on, which is a reason to measure rather than assume.

The checklist

Breaks the cacheInstead
Date or time at the top of the system promptLayer 5, at the end
Caller name or call id in the system messageLayer 5
Schema keys in map order (non-deterministic)Manifest order, always (Chapter 16)
Shuffled few-shot examplesFixed order
Per-call A/B of a layer-0 phraseSplit by deployment, not by request
Trailing whitespace that varies with the editortrim_end() — already done
In this repo

Today the system prompt is byte-identical for every caller, so the prefix is as long as it can possibly be and the hit rate should be near the theoretical maximum. This is worth measuring now, while it is trivially true, to have the baseline that shows what layering costs or saves later.

One live hazard: hot reload changes the prompt mid-flight. The turn after an edit is a guaranteed cache miss for every concurrent caller — correct behaviour, worth knowing, and a reason not to iterate on prompts against a production endpoint.

27 Streaming, and the free latency in your schema

The largest recovery available in a cascaded pipeline comes from overlapping its stages rather than speeding any of them up: stream tokens out of the model and into synthesis as they arrive, chunked at sentence boundaries. This chapter is about a version of that specific to the schema in this repository, which costs one line in a prompt file.

The observation

The schema currently emits keys in this order:

{"selected_function": ..., "confidence": ..., "language_detected": ...,
 "humanlike_sentence_answer": ..., "anger_level": ...,
 "is_hanging_up": ..., "is_greeting": ..., "requires_clarification_question": ...}

Exactly one of those keys is heard by the caller. It is fourth. Three keys are generated before the sentence starts, and four after it finishes — and generation is strictly serial, so every one of those tokens is time the line is silent.

The change

Put humanlike_sentence_answer first.

{"humanlike_sentence_answer": ..., "selected_function": ...,
 "confidence": ..., "language_detected": ..., "anger_level": ...,
 "is_hanging_up": ..., "is_greeting": ..., "requires_clarification_question": ...}

With streaming enabled, the first sentence-boundary chunk can be handed to synthesis while the remaining seven keys are still being generated. Everything after the sentence is metadata read by code, and code does not mind waiting.

Time until the caller hears anything
Non-streaming, sentence 4th (today)All ~100 tokens, then the network, then synthesis
Streaming, sentence 4th~3 keys of preamble, then the sentence
Streaming, sentence 1stThe opening brace and one key name

What it costs

Three things, all small, and one of them is already handled.

The schema order is also the badge order in the mimic client, and there is a test in vllm.rs asserting keys arrive in the order the schema lists them. Moving the answer to the front changes that order. The badge row is cosmetic and the test asserts the order matches the schema, so the fix is to update the expected order in the test — and the test correctly fails first, which is what it is for.

Parsing becomes incremental. The client currently awaits the whole body and calls serde_json::from_str. Streaming means accumulating the token stream, detecting the end of the first string value, and emitting it — while still parsing the complete object at the end for the structured fields. That is real work, and it is the only part of this change that is not free.

A truncated stream needs different handling. Today Truncated is detected from finish_reason after the fact. When streaming, the sentence may already have been spoken before the truncation is known. Which is fine — the sentence was complete; it is the metadata that was cut — but it means Truncated stops being a 502 and becomes a degraded-but-usable turn. Chapter 30.

Rule

Order the output schema by when the value is needed, not by importance or by how it reads. Anything on the critical path to the caller's ear comes first; anything consumed by code comes after. This is free, it is one line in a prompt file, and it is the only latency optimisation in this book that costs nothing.

Sentence chunking, if this is ever owned here

If synthesis is ever driven from this service rather than by the phone system, the buffer between the token stream and the synthesiser has known rules: break on sentence-ending punctuation followed by whitespace, exclude abbreviations and decimals, and enforce a minimum chunk length — around ten characters — so fragments are not sent. Word-by-word is too many requests; whole-answer is the delay this chapter exists to remove. → §IX, Chapter 49

Reliability

A phone call cannot be retried by the person on it. Four chapters on the properties that keep a turn safe when the network, the GPU or the telephony platform misbehaves — and on the one ordering decision that decides whether a caller can be told something untrue.

28   Idempotency under at-least-once delivery
29   Retries, budgets, and what must never be retried
30   The degradation ladder
31   Commit before you say it is done

28 Idempotency under at-least-once delivery

Every major webhook provider — Stripe, Shopify, GitHub, Twilio — delivers with at-least-once semantics. Duplicates are not a bug in their implementation; they are the documented guarantee. A system receiving webhooks will receive the same event two, three or more times, and the only workable posture is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent effects.

This matters here more than it does for most webhook consumers, because the duplicate is not a duplicate row in a report. It is a second booking, or the same question asked twice to a caller who already answered it.

The key

Two levels, and both are needed.

Turn level
The delivery identifier. The Standard Webhooks specification — stewarded by Svix with Twilio among its partners — standardises webhook-id, webhook-timestamp and webhook-signature, and explicitly recommends using webhook-id as the idempotency key. Twilio also sends I-Twilio-Idempotency-Token to distinguish retry attempts. Whatever the platform provides, store it with the turn and short-circuit a repeat: return the same response, do not re-run the turn.
Commit level
call_id plus a hash of the slot values being committed. This is the one that survives a caller-side retry, a load-balancer replay, or a network partition that made the first response invisible. Two commits with the same call and the same content are one commit.

Returning the cached response rather than recomputing matters: a replayed turn that goes through the model again may produce a different sentence, and the caller then hears two different answers to one question.

The 15-second ceiling

Twilio enforces a 15-second limit on webhook responses. Chapter 3's numbers say a normal turn here takes 0.6–2.8 s, so there is room — but timeout_seconds = 120 is eight times the ceiling. On the bad day the timeout was sized for, the platform has given up long before this service does, and the work continues on a GPU for a connection nobody is listening to.

Rule

The inference timeout must be shorter than the caller's own timeout. A budget longer than the platform's ceiling cannot produce a useful answer; it can only consume a GPU slot that a live caller needs. Find out the platform's limit, subtract the overhead, and size the budget under it — then let Chapter 30's ladder handle the case where that is not enough.

The general shape webhook practice recommends is queue-first: acknowledge quickly and do the work behind it. That does not apply to the turn itself — the caller is waiting for the sentence, so the work is the response — but it applies exactly to everything downstream of the answer, which is Chapter 31.

29 Retries, budgets, and what must never be retried

The classification

FailureRetry?Why
TimeoutOnce, maybeSlow, not broken — but see the budget below
Transport (connection refused)OnceFast to fail, plausibly transient
Malformed / SchemaViolationOnce, differentlyNot a plain retry — a repair prompt (Chapter 30)
TruncatedNeverDeterministic. The cap is the cause; the identical request truncates identically
Validator rejectionNeverNot a failure. It is a conversational turn
Anything already committedNeverChapter 31

The budget, not the count

“Retry twice” is the wrong policy for a caller-facing turn, because two retries of a 2.8-second call is 8.4 seconds of silence and the caller has already spoken again. The right policy is a deadline:

deadline = now + turn_budget            // what the caller will tolerate
loop {
    remaining = deadline - now
    if remaining < min_useful_attempt { break }   // no time to try again
    attempt with timeout = remaining
}
// out of budget: the ladder in chapter 30, not an error page

A retry is attempted only if there is time for it to be useful. This is the discipline the 12-Factor formulation means by owning the control flow: the application owns the loop, the stop conditions, the retries and the budget ceilings, rather than delegating them to a library's defaults.

Trap

Retrying a timeout against an overloaded inference server is how a slow system becomes an unavailable one. The first request is still occupying the GPU; the retry queues behind it; both now count against capacity. If timeouts are correlated — and under load they always are — retries multiply load precisely when load is the problem. Either do not retry timeouts, or put a circuit breaker in front of the decision.

Jitter, and why it matters on a phone line

Calls do not arrive uniformly. An outbound campaign or an IVR menu that expires produces a burst of turns within a few hundred milliseconds of each other, and a fixed backoff makes every one of them retry in unison. Full jitter — a random delay in [0, backoff] — costs nothing and breaks the synchronisation.

30 The degradation ladder

The worst outcome of any failure in this system is silence. A caller hearing nothing assumes the line dropped, starts talking, triggers barge-in, and the turn is lost regardless of what the server eventually produced.

So every failure path must terminate in a sentence. The ladder is the ordered list of ways to produce one.

#RungWhenCosts
1The answerNormalOne model call
2Repair prompt Output did not conform. Re-ask with the error and the offending output appended A second model call — only if the budget allows
3Partial extraction The sentence arrived but the metadata did not (common when streaming, Chapter 27) Nothing. Speak the sentence; treat the slots as uncollected
4Deterministic sentence No usable model output at all Nothing. A written phrase, in the right language, from a table
5Hand off Rung 4 has been used twice in this call, or the step is critical A human (Chapter 36)

Rung 2, and its limit

A repair prompt — echoing the malformed output with the parser's complaint and asking for a corrected version — has a high success rate and is the standard recovery. Two constraints: it must be inside the turn budget (Chapter 29), and it must be attempted at most once. A repair loop is indistinguishable from a hang from the caller's side.

Note that constrained decoding (Chapter 22) makes this rung largely unnecessary, which is another argument for it.

Rung 4 is the one to build first

A small table of written sentences, per language, for the handful of situations that have no model output: I'm having trouble with that, let me try again; Sorry — could you say that once more?; Let me put you through to someone who can help. They never fail, they cost nothing, and they are the floor under everything above them.

In this repo

ai_autocalls_rust has this as a first-class module — messages/phrase.rs, “every sentence, named, in every language”, with its extension guide listing “change something the caller hears” as one of the no-code tasks. ai_assistant has no equivalent: today, a VllmError becomes an ApiError and the caller's side receives {"error": "..."} with a 502 or 504, and whatever that platform does with an error response is what the caller hears.

That is a real gap and a small one to close. It is also the piece that has to exist before the timeout can safely be lowered to fit under the platform ceiling (Chapter 28), because lowering it without a fallback sentence converts slow turns into silent ones.

Rule

Never return an error to a live call. Every code path that can fail must end in a sentence in the caller's language, and the HTTP status is for the platform's logs, not for the caller's ear.

31 Commit before you say it is done

One ordering decision, stated once, because everything else in this Part is in service of it.

  1. The caller says the final yes.
  2. The submission is written to durable storage, inside the request, marked pending.
  3. Then the caller is told it is done.
  4. A background task delivers it onward and records the outcome.

Steps 2 and 3 are in that order because the booking must exist before the caller is told it does. Steps 3 and 4 are in that order because the caller must never wait on a third party: if the receiving system is slow the caller hears silence, and if it is down the caller hears a failure for something that actually succeeded.

The consequence worth stating plainly: a booking whose delivery permanently fails is still a booking. The row stays, marked failed, with the attempt count and the last error, and can be re-sent by hand. Nothing is lost, and nothing pretends to have been delivered.

Trap

The natural implementation is the wrong one. Calling the downstream API and then confirming to the caller feels more honest — only say it worked if it worked. It is not more honest; it converts a third party's latency into dead air on a phone call, and a third party's outage into a caller being told their booking failed when the data to make it is sitting in memory. The durable write is the promise; the delivery is logistics.

Where the idempotency key goes

On the submission row, as a unique constraint over (call_id, payload_hash). Then a replayed final turn (Chapter 28) hits the constraint, returns the existing row's id, and the caller hears the same confirmation. No branch, no check-then-insert race, and the database enforces it rather than the application remembering to.

In this repo

forms/delivery.rs in ai_autocalls_rust implements steps 1–4 exactly, and its module doc is the clearest statement of the reasoning in either repository — worth reading before writing the equivalent here. The one thing it does not yet have is the uniqueness constraint; save_submission is a plain INSERT. On a mimicked client that is fine. Against a telephony platform that retries webhooks, it is a duplicate booking waiting for a network blip.

Voice realities

Everything in this Part follows from one fact: the caller cannot see, cannot scroll, and cannot re-read. A spoken sentence exists for two seconds and then only in someone's memory. That constraint invalidates most of what is known about designing forms, and the discipline that replaces it is older and better documented than the model at the centre of the system.

32   The caller cannot scroll
33   Confirmation: what, and how much
34   Reading values back
35   No-match, no-input, and the third strike
36   Handing off to a human
37   Language, and staying in it

32 The caller cannot scroll

A handful of rules, each of which is a consequence of the same constraint.

One question per turn
Two questions in one sentence gets one answer, and it is ambiguous which question it answered. This is not a model limitation; it is how people respond to compound questions.
At most three options, and put them last
Recall of a spoken list collapses past three, and the last item is remembered best. “Would you like morning, afternoon, or evening?”, never a list of six times.
The question goes at the end
Context first, question last. A caller who hears the question first stops listening to the context and answers immediately.
Acknowledge, then proceed
A one-word acknowledgement before the next question tells the caller they were heard. Without it every turn feels like the system might not have registered the last one.
Never read out what belongs on a screen
Reference numbers, URLs, opening hours for seven days. If it has to be conveyed, it goes to an SMS or an email, and the call says so.

Say what is happening

The caller must always know whether the system is listening, working, or speaking. Silence is the ambiguous state and it is the one that breaks conversations — a caller who is not sure whether they were heard will speak again, and the barge-in that follows costs a whole turn. → §IX, Chapter 48

Where an action takes a noticeable time — a lookup, an availability check — the sentence that precedes it is doing real work: “Let me check that for you.” It converts dead air into an expected pause. The realtime prompting guidance calls these tool preambles and treats them as part of the tool's definition rather than as decoration, which is the right place for them.

33 Confirmation: what, and how much

Confirmations prevent mistakes and cost turns. The working principle is narrow: confirm what is expensive to get wrong, and nothing else. High-risk actions — payments, cancellations, account changes — are confirmed clearly; low-risk lookups are not confirmed at all.

The three strategies

StrategySounds likeCostsUse for
None “And how many people?” 0 turns Low-stakes, easily corrected later, high recognition confidence
Implicit “The second of October — and how many people?” 0 turns The default. Most collected slots
Explicit “That's the second of October. Is that right?” 1 turn Irreversible actions, identifiers, money, anything read from a lookup

Implicit confirmation is the technique worth internalising: the value is read back inside the next question, so the caller can object but is not required to agree. It costs nothing and catches most recognition errors, because a caller who hears the wrong date will interrupt.

The failure mode of over-confirming is not merely slowness. A caller asked “is that right?” five times stops listening and says yes reflexively, which means the sixth confirmation — the one that mattered — is worthless. Confirmation is a budget, and spending it on a party size means not having it for a payment.

Batch the explicit confirmation

Rather than confirming each field as it is collected, collect them and read the whole thing back once at the end. One turn instead of four, and the caller hears the booking as a booking rather than as a sequence of disconnected facts.

The cost is the trap from Chapter 9: the review stage must accept a correction to one field, not just a yes or a no. “No, the date's wrong” is a yes to everything else.

In this repo

ai_autocalls_rust models both: ConfirmingField { index } for per-field explicit confirmation and ReviewingSummary for the batch at the end, with form_review.rs handling the latter. Per-field confirmation is therefore a property of the field, which is where it belongs — in the manifest, next to the type and the validator (Chapter 16).

One detail from that codebase is worth copying exactly: yes/no goes through the ordinary parser, and that parser checks negatives first. “That's not right” and German “stimmt nicht” both contain a positive word. The same function confirms a date of birth and accepts a final booking, so getting the order wrong there is not a detail.

34 Reading values back

Text-to-speech engines handle ordinary prose well and handle exactly the patterns a form produces badly: identifiers, dates in regional formats, phone numbers with international prefixes, currency. These were rare in training data and are the entire output of a booking flow.

The architectural rule

The model emits structure. Code renders speech.

A model asked to produce a spoken form of a date will produce a good one most of the time. “Most of the time” is unacceptable for the one sentence whose whole purpose is letting the caller verify a value. Rendering a typed value into speech is a total function over a small set of types, it is testable, and it cannot drift.

This is the general form of the argument in forms/value.rs: read-back is a method on the value, per kind, and the compiler lists every match arm so a new answer kind cannot forget it.

The table

TypeDo not saySayMechanism
Reference codeI5DF3 “I — 5 — D — F — 3” Spell it; <say-as interpret-as="characters">
Date1987-03-05 The way that language says dates Render per locale; never emit ISO into speech
Phone number+441632960123 Grouped, with pauses <say-as interpret-as="telephone">, or insert spaces
Money42.50 “forty-two pounds fifty” Render with the currency name
ChoiceThe database valueThe human label The option list carries both
Time14:00“two in the afternoon” 24-hour clock read aloud is ambiguous in most languages

The date trap, specifically

04/05/2026 is the 4th of May in most of the world and the 5th of April in the United States. A system serving de|en|ru has three conventions in play. The resolution is that a date never exists as a formatted string inside the system — it is a date type from the moment it is parsed until the moment it is rendered, and it is rendered differently for storage, for display and for speech.

Confirm digit by digit, then check the whole

When reading an identifier back for verification, group it: “that's I, 5, D, F, 3 — I5DF3”. The spelled version is what the caller checks against the letters in front of them; the whole version is what they recognise. Either alone is worse than both.

Trap

Modern neural synthesisers normalise most text acceptably without SSML, which is why this is easy to skip in testing with clean English input. It degrades quietly: a German date read with English conventions, a reference code pronounced as a word, a price read as a decimal number. None of these raise an error and all of them produce a caller who confirms the wrong value — which is worse than a caller who could not hear it, because the system now has a confirmed wrong value.

35 No-match, no-input, and the third strike

Two failures, and they need different sentences.

No-input
Silence. They did not hear, are distracted, or the audio path failed. The right response repeats the question, usually verbatim.
No-match
They spoke and it could not be understood. The right response changes — repeating the same question is the single most frustrating behaviour a phone system has.

The escalation

AttemptNo-inputNo-match
1Repeat verbatimRephrase, shorter
2Rephrase, add the formatNarrow it: offer two or three choices, or ask for a digit
3Hand off. Do not ask a fourth time

Three is the documented convention — Dialogflow CX's voice-agent guidance is explicit about a maximum of three no-match/no-input events per page, escalating to a human on the third. It is not arbitrary: by the third failure the problem is usually the audio path, the accent, or a question the caller cannot answer, and none of those improve with a fourth attempt.

Narrowing beats repeating

Attempt 2 for a no-match should reduce the answer space, not restate the question. An open question that failed twice will fail a third time; a closed one might not.

ask:      "What date would you like?"
no-match: "Sorry - what day were you thinking of?"
no-match: "Let's try this - would you prefer this week or next?"
                                              // two options, not a date

This also changes the parser in play: a choice parser is far more forgiving than a date parser, so the narrowed question is more likely to succeed for reasons beyond the wording.

In this repo

FormProgress::attempts is this counter, and its doc comment carries the rule that is easiest to get wrong: it is not incremented when the caller asks a reasonable question instead of answering — “they did not fail, they asked something”. Without that exception, a caller who asks two clarifying questions about a form is transferred to a human for being engaged. The counter resets whenever an answer lands.

Rule

The re-prompt must differ from the prompt, and the third failure ends the attempt. Put the variety in the prompt layer as an explicit instruction plus two differently-shaped examples (Chapter 13); put the counting and the escalation in code (Chapter 8). Neither works alone.

36 Handing off to a human

The three shapes

Cold transfer
Route and disconnect. Fine for department routing where context does not matter.
Warm transfer with introduction
The agent briefs the human before connecting. The default for anything where what has already been said shapes what the human says next.
Conferenced
The system stays on the line and keeps working — notes, CRM updates, follow-up scheduling — while the human talks.

What triggers one

  • Confidence below the per-intent threshold (Chapter 23).
  • Three failures on one step (Chapter 35).
  • Sentiment — and here anger_level earns its place.
  • Policy: refunds over a limit, legal language, a vulnerable caller.
  • Elapsed time. A voice interaction running past 5–10 minutes without resolution escalates regardless of every other signal.
  • The caller asked. This one is absolute and needs no threshold.

Hand over a structure, not a paragraph

The single most actionable finding in the hand-off literature: pass structured context, not free-form notes. The human wants a card with the fields that matter — account identifier, request type, what has been tried, sentiment — because a free-form summary wastes the first thirty seconds of their attention.

call_id       9f2c-...             turns          14
caller        Maria Kovac          sentiment      frustrated (0.7)
verified      customer_id C-88213  (lookup, turn 4)
intent        reschedule_appointment
collected     date 2026-10-02 (confirmed), party_size - (3 failures)
tried         narrowed to this week / next week; both no-match
reason        attempt limit on party_size

Note the shape: it is the slot map plus provenance plus the attempt counters. Every field on that card already exists in the state designed in Part II. The hand-off card is not a feature to build later; it is a rendering of state the system already holds, which is one of the better arguments for holding it properly.

Rule

Never make the caller re-authenticate after a transfer. Re-verification after hand-off is the most common complaint about escalation, and the fix is to pass the authentication state forward as part of the card. A Verified slot (Chapter 7) is precisely the thing that can be passed with confidence — which is why the distinction was worth a type.

37 Language, and staying in it

The schema asks for language_detected with values de|en|ru, which means language is currently decided per turn. For a stateless classifier that is the only option. For a call it is the wrong default.

Sticky, with an explicit switch

The language of a call is a property of the call. Detect it on the first substantive turn, record it on the session, and use it for everything afterwards — including everything already asked. A caller who says a proper noun that reads as German should not get a German confirmation of an English booking.

Per-turn detection has a specific failure mode: short utterances. “Ja”, “OK”, “Maria Kovac” carry almost no language signal, and a per-turn detector will flip on them — usually at the confirmation step, which is the worst possible moment.

In this repo

CallSession::language in ai_autocalls_rust carries exactly this decision, with the reasoning in the field's comment: recorded on the session as well as on each request “so that a caller who switches their language selector mid-call does not end up with a form half in each — the session's language wins for anything already asked.” Keep language_detected in the schema as a signal; do not let it be the decision.

What has to be translated, and what does not

LayerMultilingual?
Deterministic fallback sentences (Chapter 30)Yes — one table per language
Value read-back rendering (Chapter 34)Yes — dates and numbers are per-locale
Option labelsYes — the label, not the stored value
The system promptNo — write it in one language and pin the output language
Slot names, function names, log fieldsNo — ever

Keeping the prompt in one language matters for the prefix cache (Chapter 26): three translated system prompts are three separate prefixes competing for the same cache. One prompt with an explicit output-language instruction is one prefix, and the instruction costs a handful of tokens.

Evaluation & observability

A system with a language model in it has no compiler for the part that matters. A one-word prompt edit can change behaviour and nothing will say so. The substitute is a measurement loop, and the reason this Part comes after the design chapters rather than before is that most of what it measures only exists once the state in Part II does.

38   Three loops
39   The metrics that matter
40   Tracing a call
41   What to log, and what must never be

38 Three loops

Different failures are caught at different speeds and at different costs. The mistake is to build only the slowest one.

LoopRuns in CatchesCannot catch
UnitMilliseconds Parsers, validators, the step predicate, read-back rendering, prompt assembly Anything about the model
ScenarioMinutes Routing, extraction, the shape of a whole dialogue, regressions from a prompt edit Real audio, real accents, real interruptions
ProductionContinuously Everything the other two do not anticipate Anything, before it reaches a caller

Loop 1 is mostly already here

The 19 library tests in this repository are a good example of what belongs in this loop, and two of them are worth naming as patterns rather than as tests.

keys_the_code_has_never_heard_of_survive_the_round_trip asserts a design property, not a behaviour: if it ever needs a Rust change to keep passing, extending the schema has stopped being free. That is a test of the architecture, and the comment says so.

a_server_that_never_answers_is_reported_as_a_timeout binds a socket, accepts, and never replies — which is what a busy vLLM looks like from the client side. It tests an error classification that would otherwise only be exercised by the incident it was written for.

Everything added in Part II belongs in this loop and is cheap to test there: a parser is a pure function from a string to an optional value, a validator is a predicate, the step predicate is a predicate, and read-back rendering is a total function over an enum.

Loop 2 is the one that does not exist yet

A scenario is a scripted conversation plus the assertions that should hold at the end: which function was selected, which slots were filled with which values, how many turns it took, whether it escalated.

scenario: reschedule, caller corrects the date mid-form
  turns:
    - say: "hi, I need to move my appointment"
      expect: { selected_function: reschedule_appointment }
    - say: "it's for the second of October"
      expect: { slot.appointment_date: 2026-10-02 }
    - say: "actually no, make it the third"
      expect: { slot.appointment_date: 2026-10-03,
                slot.appointment_date.confirmed: false }   // ch.9
  end:
    turns_taken: { max: 6 }
    escalated: false

The practical guidance on sizing: 40 to 60 scenarios is a workable starting suite, and the baseline is the recorded behaviour of the build currently trusted in production, captured as a fixed set that can be replayed against any future build. A regression in any one of them blocks the release.

Rule

The scenario suite runs on every prompt change, not only on every code change. Hot reload means a prompt edit ships without a build, which makes it the most likely source of an unreviewed regression and the least likely to be tested. A prompt edit that has not run the suite is an untested deploy.

Where an LLM judge is legitimate

Assertions on structured fields — which function, which slot value, how many turns — are exact and need no judge. Assertions on the sentence do need one, and that is where a model-graded rubric belongs: was it in the right language, did it ask exactly one question, did it avoid repeating the previous turn verbatim, did it read the date back in a spoken form.

The line: a judge is for properties of prose with no exact answer. It is not a substitute for an assertion that could have been exact. A suite that grades “did it extract the right date?” with a model has replaced a measurement with an opinion.

39 The metrics that matter

Grouped by the question they answer, because a dashboard of forty numbers answers none.

Is it working for callers

MetricNotes
Task completion rateOf calls that started a form, how many produced a submission. The headline number
Containment rateResolved without a human. Watch alongside completion — containment alone rewards refusing to escalate
Turns to completionDistribution, not mean. A long tail is where the confirmation and re-prompt problems show
Escalation rate, by triggerWhich of Chapter 36's triggers fired. A shift between triggers is the early warning

Is the model behaving

MetricNotes
JSON validity rateMalformed over total. Should be ~100% under constrained decoding
Schema conformance rateSeparate from the above — see Chapter 22
Truncation rateTruncated over total. Any non-zero value means max_tokens needs re-deriving
Routing distributionShare per selected_function. A sudden shift after a prompt edit is the fastest regression signal available
Slot extraction accuracyPer slot, against confirmed values. The slot that is always corrected is a prompt problem, not a caller problem

Is it fast enough

MetricNotes
Time to first tokenThe one comparable to the 375 ms budget (Chapter 3). Not currently measured
Total turn timep50 / p95 / p99. The mean is not useful
Prefix cache hit rateFrom vLLM. The leading indicator for time to first token (Chapter 26)
Queue depthWhere tail latency actually comes from under load
Rule

Percentiles, never means, for anything on the path to a caller's ear. A mean turn time of 1.2 s with a p95 of 6 s is a system where one call in twenty has the agent talking over the caller, and the mean says it is fine.

Offline and online are the same metrics

The pattern that works: the metrics scored in the scenario suite are the same ones charted live in production, so a regression caught offline and an incident caught online are expressed in the same units. Production data then feeds back — a call that went wrong becomes a scenario, and the suite grows from real failures rather than from imagination.

40 Tracing a call

OpenTelemetry's GenAI semantic conventions define a standard vocabulary for model invocations, tool calls and agent runs, so a span from one framework looks like a span from a raw API call. Adopting them costs almost nothing at this stage and saves a migration later.

The span tree

call            trace, id = call_id                     // the whole conversation
  turn          span, one per request
    prompt.assemble                                     // ch.18; carries the hash
    gen_ai.chat  gen_ai.request.model, .usage.*, .response.finish_reasons
    parse                                               // ch.25 error variant on failure
    slots.merge                                         // which slots changed, and from what
    step.evaluate                                       // ch.8 predicate, and its result
  turn
  ...
  submission.commit                                     // ch.31

Using call_id as the trace id is the decision that makes this useful: every turn of a call is one trace, and a support question about a call becomes a single lookup rather than a log search.

The attributes to emit

AttributeValue
gen_ai.request.modelQwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-AWQ
gen_ai.usage.input_tokens / output_tokensFrom the response
gen_ai.response.finish_reasonsThe length / stop distinction already parsed
prompt.hashChapter 18 — the binding between a call and a prompt version
form.key, form.stage, slot.nameProject-specific, and worth as much as the standard ones

Two metric instruments are worth wiring on day one: gen_ai.client.operation.duration and gen_ai.client.token.usage, both histograms. Between them they cover most of Chapter 39's third table.

Rule

Prompts and messages go in span events, not span attributes. Attributes are indexed and retained on every span; the content is large, variable, and — in this system — personal data. Events can be sampled, dropped and redacted independently, which is the whole of Chapter 41.

In this repo

tracing is already in the stack, rolling daily to LOG_DIR with ANSI off, and main.rs loads settings before initialising it because LOG_DIR decides where logging goes. Adding tracing-opentelemetry is a subscriber layer, not a rewrite.

One trap is already documented and worth re-reading: .env had three RUST_LOG lines, and the last one won — mwf=trace,tower_http=debug, naming a crate this project does not have, which filters out the application's own logs. Harmless while tracing initialised first; it would have made the new log files empty. The general lesson is that a filter naming a crate that does not exist fails silently and produces a system that looks healthy because it says nothing.

41 What to log, and what must never be

The known gap, from context.md:

request_text is logged verbatim. On real calls that is personal data (GDPR retention/erasure). Redact before this touches a phone line. ai_assistant, context.md — Known gaps

That assessment is correct and Part VIII is the full treatment. This chapter is the operational half: what a log line should contain so that it is useful without being a liability.

The three tiers

TierContentsRetention
Always call_id, turn number, stage, selected function, slot names changed, latency, token counts, error variant, prompt hash Ordinary operational retention. Contains no caller content
Redacted Utterance and generated sentence with entities masked: "my name is [PERSON] and my reference is [ID]" Short. Justified, documented, enforced (Chapter 44)
Never Raw utterance, raw slot values, the assembled prompt, the API key, anything marked Verified —

The first tier is the one that does the diagnostic work. Chapter 16's scenario — a slot renamed in one place — is fully diagnosable from slot names and the predicate's result, with no caller content at all: a step that keeps re-asking with an unchanged slot map is visible in the structure of the trace.

Trap

The debug log written during development is the one that leaks. debug!(content, truncated, "vLLM answered") in vllm.rs logs the model's complete output — which is exactly what is wanted while iterating on a prompt, and which contains the caller's name, their date of birth and their reference number the moment this is on a real line. It is gated behind RUST_LOG, and RUST_LOG=debug gets set in production by someone diagnosing an incident at two in the morning.

Redaction belongs in the field, not in the level. A value that must not be logged should be a type whose Debug and Display print [redacted], so no log level can reveal it and no future call site can forget.

Rule

Log the shape of the turn, not its contents. Slot names, not slot values. Which function, not what they said. A prompt hash, not a prompt. Every one of those is enough to debug the class of failure it belongs to, and none of them is personal data.

Compliance & data

The only Part that can stop the project rather than degrade it. Four chapters on obligations that are architectural rather than procedural — things that have to be designed in, because retrofitting them means rewriting the storage layer and re-processing everything already collected.

42   request_text is personal data
43   Redaction as architecture
44   Retention, erasure, and the call_id index
45   Disclosure: the caller must be told

This Part describes engineering obligations that follow from published regulation and industry practice. It is not legal advice, and the scope of what applies depends on where callers are, what the calls are for, and who the controller is. Every item here is something an engineer must build; whether it is sufficient is a question for whoever signs off the processing.

42 request_text is personal data

The claim is not that call transcripts might contain personal data. Under GDPR, voice recordings are personal data, and a voiceprint is biometric data in the special category of Article 9, requiring explicit consent and stricter controls than ordinary text. A transcript of what a caller said is personal data about that caller from the first word.

Which means the things this system does with request_text are processing operations:

What happens todayWhat it is
Arrives in a POST bodyCollection
Sent to vLLM in a promptProcessing; the inference server is in scope
Logged verbatim to ./logs/app.log.<date>Storage — needs a retention period
Rolls daily on a mounted volumeStorage with no expiry, currently unbounded
(Planned) held in a Redis sessionStorage — the TTL is the retention period
(Planned) written into a submissionStorage, durable, with the longest life of any of these

The one that stands out is the log volume. tracing-appender rotates daily and does not delete; .gitignore ignores rotated logs and logs/.gitkeep keeps the mount point. So the current retention period for verbatim caller utterances is forever, on a host directory, with no deletion mechanism.

That is fine today, because the callers are the developer testing through the mimic client. It stops being fine on the first real call, and the fix is cheapest before there is anything to re-process.

The inference server is in scope too

A locally hosted model is a significant advantage here: nothing leaves the machine, there is no third-party processor to contract with, and no international transfer question. That is worth stating explicitly in whatever record of processing activities this ends up in, because it removes a whole class of obligation that a hosted API would create.

It does not remove the obligation to know what the inference server logs. A vLLM instance started with request logging enabled writes prompts to its own stdout, which the container runtime keeps, in a place nobody has applied a retention policy to.

43 Redaction as architecture

Real-time redaction prevents personal data from ever reaching storage. Compliance is architectural.

The distinction that matters: redacting on the way in is a property of the system; redacting on the way out is a promise that every reader honours a policy. The second one fails the first time somebody greps a log file or copies a value into a ticket.

Where the boundary goes

utterance arrives
     |
     +--> [ recogniser ] ---> named entities found
     |
     +--> redacted copy  ---> logs, traces, metrics, analytics, tickets
     |
     +--> raw copy       ---> the model, and the slot parsers
                              lives for the turn; never written down

The raw text has to reach the model — a system that redacts the name before extraction cannot extract the name. So the boundary is not “redact everything everywhere”; it is the raw text exists in memory for the duration of a turn and is never persisted, while everything durable sees the redacted copy.

The mechanism is a named-entity recogniser running on the transcript stream, masking or tokenising before the text reaches the log pipeline, the analytics store or a CRM.

What the slot map changes

Part II's design helps here in a way that is easy to miss. Once values live in a typed slot map, the system does not need the raw utterance anymore. It needs a date, a party size and a reference code, and those are typed values with known sensitivity, stored under known names, that can be individually classified, individually redacted and individually deleted.

Raw utteranceTyped slot
Classify sensitivityRequires NER, per instanceFrom the manifest, once per slot
Redact for a logRequires NER, per instanceA flag on the slot definition
Delete on requestFind it in free textDelete a field
Retain selectivelyAll or nothingPer slot, per purpose

Which gives the storage rule: keep the raw string for the length of the call (Chapter 7 wanted it for corrections and diagnosis) and let it expire with the session. Persist only typed values, and only those the submission actually needs.

Rule

Mark sensitivity in the manifest, next to the type. A slot is ordinary, sensitive or special-category, and that classification drives logging, retention and what appears in a hand-off card — automatically, from one declaration. Chapter 16's “one manifest, two consumers” becomes three.

Trap

Redacting the transcript and keeping the audio is not redaction. Where a recording exists, the audio itself has to have the segments removed, not just the text record. That is the phone platform's problem rather than this service's — but it is the kind of thing that is assumed to be handled by whoever is not handling it, and it is worth a written answer from the platform rather than an assumption.

44 Retention, erasure, and the call_id index

Retention

Quality-assurance retention for call data typically runs 30 to 90 days in practice. The number matters less than three properties: the period is justified (there is a reason it is 60 days and not 600), documented, and enforced automatically by the system rather than by somebody remembering to run a cleanup.

StorePeriodEnforced by
Redis call sessionHoursTTL — automatic, already correct in principle
Application logsDaysNothing today. Needs a rotation-and-delete policy
TracesDaysThe collector's policy
SubmissionsThe business purposeA scheduled job — and the longest-lived data here
Measure this

cache_settings.session_ttl_days = 1 is the only retention period currently expressed anywhere in the configuration, and it is expressed in days for data whose useful life is minutes. When the call session is built on top of it, that unit is the difference between a personal data footprint measured in an hour and one measured in a day. Chapter 10 made the operational argument; this is the compliance one, and they point the same way.

Erasure needs an index, and indexes are designed in

A caller asks for their data to be deleted. To honour that, every store has to be searchable by something the caller can be identified with.

This is the practical argument for using the phone system's call_id everywhere (Chapter 10) and for it being the trace id (Chapter 40). One identifier reaches the session, the submission, the logs and the traces. Without that discipline, erasure means a free-text search across a log volume, which is neither complete nor verifiable.

Rule

Every store that holds caller data carries the call_id as an indexed field, and there is one function that deletes a call from all of them. Write it before it is needed — a deletion path invented under a deadline is a deletion path that misses a store.

A useful consequence: if the redaction boundary in Chapter 43 holds, most of what would otherwise have to be found and deleted does not exist. The log tier that carries no caller content needs no erasure path, which is the cheapest possible way to satisfy the obligation.

45 Disclosure: the caller must be told

Article 50 of the EU AI Act took effect on 2 August 2026 and applies where people interact directly with an AI system. For a voice agent, the reported requirement is specific in a way that is unusual for regulation: the disclosure must be audible, in plain language, at the latest at the first interaction — not on a terms page, not on a screen the caller may not see, but spoken as part of the interaction.

Two facts have to be conveyed: that the caller is talking to a machine, and on whose behalf.

What that means for this design

It is a first-turn requirement, which makes it a state question rather than a prompt question.

  • The disclosure belongs to the call, not the turn. It happens once, and the fact that it happened is recorded on the session.
  • It must not be generated. The wording is a compliance artefact: it is reviewed, it is fixed, and it is per language. This is a phrase.rs entry (Chapter 30), not a humanlike_sentence_answer.
  • It must survive the failure paths. A call that starts with a timeout must not skip it and disclose on turn two, so the disclosure is emitted before the first model call is made, not after it succeeds.
  • It should be logged — with the call id and the exact text — because “we disclose” is a claim and a log line is evidence.
In this repo

ai_autocalls_rust has the hook already: CallEvent::CallStarted, whose comment says it exists “so a call has a beginning in the logs, and so a future greeting has somewhere to live”. That is where this goes. ai_assistant has no equivalent, because it has no notion of a call beginning — which is one more reason the call session in Part II is a prerequisite for going anywhere near a real phone line.

The neighbouring obligations

Three more things are worth knowing about before a real call happens, each of which is somebody's decision rather than an engineering choice, and each of which has an engineering consequence:

Recording consent
Several EU jurisdictions require all-party consent to record. If calls are recorded, consent is captured before recording starts, which means the disclosure turn and the consent turn interact.
Lawful basis
Whatever it is — contract, legitimate interests, consent — it determines what may be retained and for how long, which is the input to Chapter 44's table rather than an output of it.
The human alternative
Independently of regulation, a caller who asks for a human gets one (Chapter 36). This is the cheapest possible mitigation for a large class of risk and it is already in the design.
Rule

Build the disclosure before the first production call, not before the launch date. It is one phrase per language and one flag on the session, and it is the only item in this book that is both trivial to implement and capable of invalidating every call made without it.

The audio layer
around you

This service receives text. Someone else does the listening and the speaking. These four chapters are here because that someone else sets the latency budget you are spending, explains why transcripts arrive the way they do, and decides what “the caller said” even means when they interrupted halfway through — and because the layer may one day be yours.

46   What speech recognition hands you
47   Turn detection, and the silence you pay for
48   Barge-in, and what the caller actually heard
49   Synthesis, telephony, and owning this one day

46 What speech recognition hands you

The string in request_text has already been through a lossy process, and knowing its shape explains several things that otherwise look like model failures.

The stream, and its three kinds of result

A streaming recogniser emits interim hypotheses continuously and marks some results final. The distinction that matters is that a final segment is not necessarily the end of the turn: long utterances produce several finalised segments before the recogniser signals that speech is actually over.

SignalMeans
interim hypothesisBest guess so far. Will change. Useful for speculative work, never for a decision
final segmentThis span of audio is settled. More may follow in the same turn
end of speechThe turn is over. This is what produces a request to this service

What it does to the text

  • Punctuation is inferred, and often absent. A prompt that depends on sentence boundaries is depending on a guess.
  • Numbers arrive inconsistently — “twenty twenty-six”, “2026”, “20 26” for the same utterance. Parsers must accept words and digits for the same value, which is why a dedicated number parser exists rather than str::parse::<i64>.
  • Disfluencies survive. “uh”, “I mean — no, the”. This is the input the model is genuinely good at and a grammar never was.
  • Homophone errors are confident. “to” / “two”, “for” / “four”. The recogniser is not uncertain, it is wrong, so there is no confidence signal to catch it. This is precisely why read-back (Chapter 34) exists.
  • Names and codes are worst. Proper nouns and alphanumeric identifiers have no language model support. Anything in this class needs explicit confirmation, always.
Rule

Never treat the transcript as what the caller said. Treat it as the recogniser's best guess at what the caller said. Every design decision downstream — confirmation strategy, parser tolerance, the three-strike rule — follows from taking that seriously.

Eager end-of-turn

Some recognisers emit a speculative end-of-turn signal before the real one, so the language model can start prefilling. It costs 50–70% more model calls — some are cancelled — and saves 100–200 ms.

Worth knowing because it changes the traffic this service sees: requests that are cancelled mid-flight, and occasionally two requests for one turn. Both are things Chapter 28's idempotency handles, and neither is obvious until it appears in a metric as a mysterious inflation of turn count.

47 Turn detection, and the silence you pay for

Deciding when the caller has finished is the largest latency item in the whole pipeline, and none of it is compute.

Three approaches

MethodHowLatencyFails when
VAD only Classify each audio frame as speech or not; end the turn after N ms of silence Worst — you wait out the full threshold every turn The caller pauses mid-thought
STT endpointing Watch the transcript stream for completion signals rather than audio silence Middle. Does not need the full trailing pause Depends entirely on the recogniser's tuning
Model-based A small classifier reads partial transcripts and predicts whether the thought is finished Best — can fire before trailing silence False positives on incomplete sentences

STT endpointing is the recommended default for most production agents. Model-based detection is the low-latency option — LiveKit ships a ~135M-parameter fine-tune that runs locally and predicts whether the current transcript looks like a finished thought, combined with acoustic VAD for pacing.

The number that matters

An 800 ms silence timeout adds nearly a full second to every single response before the pipeline starts. Against Chapter 3's 1,115 ms total budget, that one setting can consume most of it.

The thresholds are tuned per vertical, and the published starting points are worth knowing even when someone else owns the dial:

ContextSilence before end-of-turn
IVR replacement — short, known answers~250 ms
Sales — conversational, longer turns~400 ms
Healthcare intake — considered answers, thinking pauses~600 ms
In this repo

This is the most valuable question to ask whoever operates the phone platform, because it is the largest number in the budget and it is a configuration value rather than an engineering project. The answer also tells you which threshold this service's own latency is competing against: a 250 ms endpoint leaves far less headroom for a 2.8-second turn than a 600 ms one does.

Trap

Turn detection interacts with the design in Chapter 32 in a way that is easy to miss. A question that invites a considered answer — “what date would suit you?” — produces thinking pauses, which a short threshold cuts in half, which produces a no-match, which produces a re-prompt. The fix is sometimes in the prompt: a more closed question produces a shorter, more fluent answer. A no-match problem is not always a recognition problem.

48 Barge-in, and what the caller actually heard

Barge-in is the caller speaking while the agent is talking. Handling it means keeping turn detection active during playback, and cancelling synthesis the moment caller speech is detected.

Turn detection decides when speech started or ended; interruption handling decides what to do about it while the agent is mid-sentence. They are separate problems and are often conflated.

The part that reaches this service

The agent said: “I have you down for the second of October at three o'clock, for four people — shall I confirm that?”

The caller interrupted after “second of October at”.

The conversation history must now record what was heard, not what was generated. If it records the full sentence, the system believes it read back a time and a party size that the caller never heard, and will treat a subsequent “yes” as confirming all of it.

Platforms expose this: on interruption, a synthesis API reports how much audio played, the text actually spoken, and the text left unspoken.

Rule

A value is confirmed only if the caller heard it read back. When the platform reports a barge-in, the turn window records the spoken prefix, and any slot whose read-back fell in the unspoken remainder stays unconfirmed. A confirmation flag set from a sentence nobody finished hearing is a false record, and it is exactly the kind that surfaces as a disputed booking.

Whether this information reaches this service is a platform question, and it is worth asking early. If it does not, the conservative fallback is to treat any barge-in as invalidating every confirmation in that turn — which costs a turn and is always safe.

Backchannels are not interruptions

“Mm-hm”, “yeah”, “right” spoken over the agent are acknowledgements, not attempts to take the floor. Treating them as barge-in produces an agent that stops every time the caller signals they are listening — which trains the caller into silence, and silence is what Chapter 47's thresholds are waiting for.

49 Synthesis, telephony, and owning this one day

Synthesis

The smallest slice of the budget — 100 ms in Twilio's allocation, and streaming systems have reported first audio as low as 80 ms through interleaved text-audio generation, which means response length does not increase initial latency.

The two things that matter from here: streaming synthesis, which starts producing audio from partial text, and the chunking rule between the model's token stream and it — sentence boundaries, excluding abbreviations and decimals, with a minimum chunk length so fragments are not sent. That is the mechanism Chapter 27's schema reorder feeds.

Operational details that bite: streaming sessions expire (two hours in one documented case), need periodic keep-alives, and reconnection resets prosody state mid-call.

Telephony

ConstraintConsequence
8 kHz, μ-law or A-lawHalf the bandwidth of consumer speech. Recognition is measurably worse than a laptop microphone; tune expectations to it
Packet loss and jitterDropped words with no error signal. Looks like a caller who mumbled
DTMFKeypad entry. The right escape hatch for a reference code that has failed twice — “you can type it in” beats a third attempt
Webhook retriesChapter 28
Response deadline15 s on one major platform. Chapter 28

DTMF deserves more attention than it usually gets. It has a 100% recognition rate, it works for callers in noisy places and for accents the recogniser handles badly, and offering it after two failures is often better than any amount of prompt engineering.

If this layer ever becomes yours

Two open frameworks dominate, and they have converged on the same shape. Pipecat models an agent as a pipeline of processors through which typed frames flow — audio chunks, transcript fragments, tokens, interruption signals — with each processor handling the frame types it understands and passing the rest through. LiveKit Agents builds on a WebRTC transport with turn detection, interruption handling and a large plugin set.

Both give you turn detection, barge-in and the streaming plumbing, and both leave everything in Parts II–VIII entirely to you. That is the useful observation: adopting one of them does not change the dialogue layer, the prompt layer, the serving layer or the compliance obligations. It replaces the boundary, not the system.

Rule

Do not build this layer. The components that make a cascade work — low-latency recognition, expressive synthesis, semantic turn detection — are where the specialist providers differentiate, and none of them is where this project's value is. Keep the boundary at text in, sentence out, and keep it clean enough that the thing on the other side can be replaced.

and vocabulary

The sources, the checklists, and the vocabulary — the parts of the book meant to be looked up rather than read.
