A Annotated bibliography

How to read this list. Entries marked ● were read in full while compiling this book. The rest were consulted through search summaries — enough to source a specific claim, not enough to recommend the whole document unseen. Where a figure in the text comes from a source, it comes from one of these; nothing is cited that was not actually retrieved. Anything described as measured on this machine comes from context.md and is not in this list.

Voice agent architecture and latency  Part I, Chapter 3

● Deepgram — Voice Agent Architecture: STT, LLM and TTS Pipeline Design
The single best source for the latency budget. Carries Twilio's 350/375/100 ms allocation and the 1,115 ms mouth-to-ear target, the observation that most recognition delay is endpointing rather than acoustic compute, and a clear bundled-versus-composed comparison table. Read the “every response accumulates three budgets” framing; skip the product specifics. deepgram.com/learn/voice-agent-architecture-stt-llm-tts-pipeline-design
Deepgram — Speech-to-Speech vs Cascade
The architecture decision stated as a decision. Source for “cascade for five or more tools with strict schema enforcement”. deepgram.com/learn/speech-to-speech-vs-cascade-voice-agent-architecture
Gradium — Cascaded Voice Agents vs Speech-to-Speech: Architecture Tradeoffs in 2026
Where the 300–500 ms versus 600–1,200 ms time-to-first-audio comparison comes from, plus the note that hybrids are emerging as a middle ground. gradium.ai/content/cascaded-voice-agent-vs-speech-to-speech-2026
AssemblyAI — Voice Agent Architecture, and The voice AI stack for building agents
Two overlapping overviews. The first is the better one on cascading versus streaming and the 3×–5× perceived-latency claim; the second is a survey of the provider landscape and dates quickly. assemblyai.com/blog/voice-agent-architecture
LiveKit — Voice agent architecture: STT, LLM and TTS pipelines explained
The clearest diagram-level explanation of the cascade. Pairs with their sequential-pipeline post, which is about ordering the stages. livekit.com/blog/voice-agent-architecture-stt-llm-tts-pipelines-explained
ElevenLabs — Voice agent latency optimization
The techniques rather than the architecture: streaming, sentence chunking, overlapping stages. Source for the sentence-buffer rules in Chapter 49 — punctuation plus whitespace, exclude abbreviations and decimals, minimum chunk length. elevenlabs.io/blog/voice-agent-latency-optimization
arXiv 2508.04721 — Toward Low-Latency End-to-End Voice Agents for Telecommunications
Streaming ASR, quantised LLMs and real-time TTS in a telecoms setting. The closest published work to this project's shape; useful if the whole pipeline is ever brought in-house. arxiv.org/html/2508.04721v1

Prompt lifecycle  Chapter 18

LaunchDarkly — Prompt versioning and management; Agenta — Prompt versioning: the complete guide
Two statements of the same consensus: prompts in git, one per file, reviewed like code, pinned to exact versions in production, templated rather than string-concatenated, and decoupled from the deployment cycle. This project already does the hard half; these are useful for the parts it does not yet do. launchdarkly.com/blog/prompt-versioning-and-management/  ·  agenta.ai/blog/prompt-versioning-guide

In-repository sources

● H:\rust\ai_autocalls_rust
The most useful reference in this list, because it is a working implementation of Part II by the same author. In reading order: app/src/events/mod.rs (the whole call flow as one enum, with the vocabulary and the naming rule), docs/EXTENDING.md (what can be added without writing code), app/src/call/session.rs (what a call remembers and why Redis), app/src/forms/flow.rs (the stage machine), app/src/forms/value.rs (typed answers and per-kind read-back), app/src/forms/delivery.rs (commit before you say it is done), app/src/forms/parsers/ (one file per answer kind).
● H:\rust\ai_assistant — context.md and the source
Every measured number attributed to “this machine” comes from context.md: the 0.6–2.8 s turn times, the 30-second timeout incident, the hot-reload byte counts, the RUST_LOG trap. app/src/vllm.rs is the best-documented file in either repository and the style model for this book.

B Checklists and decision tables

The operational half of the book: the thirty-five rules in one place, four checklists for the things that are done repeatedly, a triage table for when something breaks, and every configured value with the reasoning that produced it.

B.1   The rules, collected

Ch.Rule
1The model extracts and the model phrases. Code decides.
2Design as though the components around you will be replaced, because in a cascade they are.
3Keep three latency numbers: a target, an alert threshold, and a timeout. This project has only the third.
5Do not invent vocabulary for “a thing the call needs to collect”. Use slot, form, step, validator, confirmation, no-match.
6Extract once, store forever. A value changes only through an explicit correction, never by re-reading the transcript.
7A Verified slot has a constructor only the lookup code can reach. A model must never be able to write one.
8A step transition is a pure function of stored state. No model call, no network call, no clock.
10Write what must survive to durable storage before telling the caller it is done, and never make the caller wait on a third party.
12Order prompt layers most-static to most-volatile. Anything that changes per turn goes last, in the user message.
15Layer 5 is generated by code from state that code owns. Nothing in it is written by hand.
16Render the prompt's schema and the code's validator from the same manifest. Never maintain them side by side.
17Ask of every capability: if the caller could choose this one freely, what would it cost? That is the real authorisation model.
18Assemble and validate prompts at load; cache by (form, step); reload on a signal, not per turn.
18Log a hash of the assembled prompt on every turn. With hot reload, the file in git is not evidence of what ran.
21Re-derive max_tokens whenever a key is added to the schema, and record the measurement next to the value.
22Schemas must be stable and few, with a deterministic key order, so the number of distinct grammars equals the number of steps.
23A confidence threshold is a fitted parameter, valid for one (model, prompt, schema) triple. A prompt edit invalidates it.
25One error variant per distinct operator response, not per distinct code path.
27Order the output schema by when the value is needed. The caller's sentence first; everything code reads after.
28The inference timeout must be shorter than the caller's own timeout.
29Retry against a deadline, not a count. Attempt again only if there is time for it to be useful.
30Never return an error to a live call. Every failing path ends in a sentence in the caller's language.
33Confirm what is expensive to get wrong, and nothing else. Confirmation is a budget.
34The model emits structure; code renders speech. Read-back is a method on the value, per type.
35The re-prompt must differ from the prompt, and the third failure ends the attempt.
36Never make the caller re-authenticate after a transfer. Pass the authentication state forward.
39Percentiles, never means, for anything on the path to a caller's ear.
40Prompts and messages go in span events, not span attributes.
41Log the shape of the turn, not its contents. Slot names, not slot values.
43Mark sensitivity in the manifest, next to the type, and let it drive logging, retention and hand-off automatically.
44Every store that holds caller data carries an indexed call_id, and one function deletes a call from all of them.
45Build the disclosure before the first production call. One phrase per language, one flag on the session.
46Never treat the transcript as what the caller said. It is the recogniser's best guess.
48A value is confirmed only if the caller heard it read back.
49Do not build the audio layer. Keep the boundary at text in, sentence out.

B.2   Adding a slot

  • Declared in the form manifest: name, type, required, confirmation policy, sensitivity ch. 16, 43
  • A parser exists for its type, with unit tests for words and digits ch. 46
  • Domain validation on the type; business validation on the form — and they produce different sentences ch. 8
  • Read-back rendering implemented for its type, in every supported language ch. 34
  • Provenance decided: Verified, Collected or Inferred ch. 7
  • If Inferred: what recomputes it when its inputs change ch. 9
  • Included in the step's extraction schema and in the form-wide schema, so over-answering works ch. 9
  • max_tokens re-derived against the larger schema ch. 21
  • A scenario covers it, including one where the caller corrects it ch. 38
  • It appears on the hand-off card ch. 36
  • Its retention and deletion are covered by the existing paths ch. 44

B.3   Adding a key to the output schema

  • Decide which side of the line it is on. Read by a human → the flattened map. Drives a branch → the manifest, with a named field and a test ch. 16
  • Written as real JSON with quoted keys, in the prompt file prompts/README.md
  • Placed after humanlike_sentence_answer in schema order ch. 27
  • Token cost estimated; max_tokens re-derived ch. 21
  • The key-order test in vllm.rs updated, deliberately ch. 27
  • The scenario suite re-run — a schema change is a behaviour change ch. 38
  • If it will gate anything: calibrated first, not assumed ch. 23

B.4   Editing a prompt

  • Not against a production endpoint — every edit is a cache miss for every concurrent caller ch. 26
  • Nothing volatile moved towards the front ch. 26
  • The change addresses an observed failure, not an imagined one ch. 14
  • Sample phrases: are there now three of the same shape? ch. 13
  • The scenario suite run afterwards. A prompt edit is an untested deploy until it has been. ch. 38
  • Routing distribution checked for a shift ch. 39
  • Any confidence threshold fitted against the old prompt re-fitted ch. 23
  • Committed — hot reload means the running prompt can diverge from the repository silently ch. 18

B.5   Before the first real call

Ordered by what is hardest to retrofit.

  • Disclosure. Spoken, plain language, first interaction, naming the machine and on whose behalf. Logged ch. 45
  • Redaction boundary. Raw text lives for the turn; everything durable sees the redacted copy ch. 43
  • Log retention. ./logs rotates but never deletes; today's retention period is forever ch. 42, 44
  • The debug! that logs the model's full output is gated by level, and the level gets raised at 2 a.m. Make it a redacting type ch. 41
  • Deterministic fallback sentences exist, per language. Nothing may return an error to a call ch. 30
  • Timeout under the platform ceiling — but not before the fallback exists ch. 28, 30
  • Idempotency on the turn and a unique constraint on the submission ch. 28, 31
  • Session TTL in hours, not days ch. 10, 44
  • Erasure path that reaches every store, written before it is needed ch. 44
  • Hand-off works, carries the structured card, and does not re-authenticate ch. 36
  • Time-to-first-token and p95 turn time measured, not inferred ch. 3, 39
  • Ask the platform: end-of-turn silence threshold, webhook response ceiling, whether barge-in reports what was actually spoken ch. 47, 28, 48
  • sqlx::migrate! — still commented out in main.rs context.md

B.6   Incident triage

SymptomMost likely causeFirst thing to check
504, latency matches timeout_seconds exactly The client gave up; the server is slow, not down GPU contention and queue depth. Not container health ch. 25
502 with Transport Genuinely unreachable Container, LLM_URL, the compose network
502 with Truncated Our own cap. The schema outgrew it llm_settings.max_tokens — the message names it ch. 21
502 with Malformed Prompt or decoding mode Whether the schema is still valid JSON with quoted keys ch. 22
A badge vanished from the client The model renamed a key, or preserve_order was dropped The raw content in a debug log; then Cargo.toml ch. 16
The same question asked repeatedly; the caller is cooperating Slot name mismatch between prompt and validator Whether both come from one manifest. This is the Chapter 16 bug ch. 16
Escalations rose after a prompt edit Routing shifted; attempts now accumulate Routing distribution before and after; the prompt hash ch. 18, 39
Turn latency crept up with no code change Prefix cache hit rate collapsed Whether anything volatile moved forward in the prompt ch. 26
Callers talk over the agent p95 turn time past the budget; the timeout hides it p95, not the mean. Barge-in counts on the platform's side ch. 3, 39
A confirmed value turns out to be wrong Barge-in cut the read-back before that value was spoken Whether confirmation is set from generated or heard text ch. 48
Duplicate submissions Webhook retry; at-least-once is the guarantee The unique constraint on (call_id, payload_hash) ch. 28, 31
Log files are empty A RUST_LOG filter naming a crate that does not exist .env for duplicate RUST_LOG lines — the last wins context.md
Answers went strange after an editor save A half-saved prompt; the last good text is in use The warning line from SystemPrompt::current() ch. 18

B.7   Every configured value, and where it came from

SettingNowDerivation, and when to revisit
llm_settings.timeout_seconds120 Sized for a cold or contended GPU measured at 30 s+, not for the good case. Must drop below the platform's webhook ceiling once fallback sentences exist ch. 28, 30
llm_settings.max_tokens256 ~2.5× a ~100-token answer for eight schema keys. Re-derive on every schema change ch. 21
llm_settings.temperature0.0 Deterministic routing. Get phrasing variety from the prompt, not from this ch. 20
cache_settings.session_ttl_days1 A cookie-session value. For call sessions, express in hours — it is a retention period ch. 10, 44
database_settings.timeout_seconds3 Fine. Note it is inside the turn budget, so a slow lookup spends the caller's patience ch. 29
llm_system_prompt_filepath Relative to the working directory. Changing which file still needs a restart ch. 18
RUST_LOGone line Consolidated to info,sqlx=warn,tower_http=info. Keep it one line B.6
Turn target latencyabsent Should be ~375 ms to first token. Nothing records it today ch. 3
p95 alert thresholdabsent The number that predicts callers interrupting ch. 3, 39
Log retentionabsent Currently unbounded. 30–90 days is the convention, justified and automated ch. 44
No-match limitabsent Three, then hand off ch. 35
Turn window lengthabsent Four to six turns, fixed ch. 6, 15

C Glossary

Terms as this book uses them, including the ones these two repositories invented. Where a word has a settled meaning in the task-oriented dialogue literature, that meaning is the one given.

active fields
(this project) The list of questions currently being worked through. Not always the form's own fields — a caller who chose to be looked up is asked identity questions first. ch. 11
at-least-once delivery
The guarantee every major webhook platform provides: an event will arrive, and may arrive more than once. Duplicates are the contract, not a defect. ch. 28
barge-in
The caller speaking while the agent is talking. Handling it means cancelling synthesis and reconciling the conversation record to what was actually heard. ch. 48
backchannel
“Mm-hm”, “right” — an acknowledgement spoken over the agent, not an attempt to take the floor. Not a barge-in. ch. 48
call session
(this project) Everything known about a call in progress: language, slots collected, which question is outstanding, attempts, the turn window. Lives in Redis and expires. ch. 10
cascade / cascaded pipeline
Speech recognition, then a language model, then speech synthesis, as separate components. The dominant production architecture, and the one this service is the middle of. ch. 2
constrained decoding
Masking tokens during generation so output cannot leave a grammar. In vLLM: json_object (valid JSON), guided_json (your schema), guided_choice (one of a list). ch. 22
containment
The share of calls resolved without a human. Meaningless without task completion beside it — refusing to escalate maximises it. ch. 39
dialogue state tracking (DST)
Deriving the current slot values from a conversation. A benchmarked task; see joint goal accuracy. ch. 6
endpointing
Deciding the caller has finished, from the transcript stream rather than from audio silence. Faster than waiting out a silence threshold; the recommended default. ch. 47
event / subscriber / dispatcher
(this project) A fact about the call, the code that asked to hear about it, and the thing that routes one to the other in priority order. The observer pattern applied to a call flow. ch. 11
flow
(this project) The form currently being filled in, if any. Lives on the call session. ch. 11
form
A group of slots collected together. VoiceXML's word, and every subsequent system's. Dialogflow CX calls it a page. ch. 5
Form Interpretation Algorithm (FIA)
VoiceXML's procedure for visiting each unfilled field until the form is complete. The algorithm every slot-filling implementation converges on. ch. 5
implicit confirmation
Reading a value back inside the next question, so the caller can object without being required to agree. Costs no turns. The default. ch. 33
joint goal accuracy
The fraction of turns at which every slot is simultaneously correct. 25.65% for the best tracker on SpokenWOZ — the number behind Chapter 6's central rule. ch. 6
layer (prompt)
(this book) One of six bands of prompt content ordered by how often it changes, from identity (layer 0) to per-turn runtime state (layer 5). ch. 12
manifest
(this book) The single definition of a form's slots, types, validators and prompts, from which both the prompt's schema text and the code's validators are rendered. ch. 16
mixed initiative
The caller may answer several fields at once, in any order, without waiting to be asked. VoiceXML's term. ch. 9
no-input / no-match
Silence, and speech that could not be understood. Two different failures needing two different responses. Three of either ends the attempt. ch. 35
pass-through map
(this project) ActionDecision's flattened serde_json::Map, carrying every schema key except the one the code names. Makes schema keys free to add, and invisible to the compiler. ch. 1, 16
prefix cache
vLLM's reuse of attention state for a shared prompt prefix. Cached in 16-token blocks; keyed from position zero; worth 60–80% of time to first token when it hits. ch. 26
provenance
(this book) Where a slot's value came from: Verified (an authoritative source), Collected (the caller), Inferred (computed). The distinction that separates a bug from a data-protection incident. ch. 7
repair prompt
Re-asking the model with its malformed output and the parser's complaint attached. Rung 2 of the degradation ladder; at most once, inside the budget. ch. 30
slot
One thing the call needs to collect. VoiceXML's field item variable, Dialogflow's parameter. Here: a name, a typed value, a raw string, provenance, a confirmation flag and an attempt count. ch. 7
stage
(this project) Where a call is inside a form: confirming the start, collecting field N, confirming field N, reviewing the summary. ch. 11
step predicate
(this book) filled && valid && (!needs_confirm || confirmed), evaluated in code over stored state. Never asked of the model. ch. 8
time to first token (TTFT)
How long until generation begins. The figure comparable to the 375 ms model-stage budget, and the one this project does not currently measure. ch. 3, 39
turn
One request and one response — the caller said something, the system said something back. The unit everything in this book is measured in.
turn window
(this book) A fixed-length ring of the last four to six turns, rendered into layer 5. Evidence for reference resolution, never a source of state. ch. 6, 15
VAD (voice activity detection)
Classifying audio frames as speech or silence. The simplest turn-detection method and the slowest, because it waits out the full silence threshold every turn. ch. 47
warm transfer
Handing a call to a human with a briefing first, carrying a structured card rather than a free-form summary — and without re-authenticating the caller. ch. 36
workflow (vs. agent)
Models and tools orchestrated through predefined code paths, as against a model directing its own process. This system is a workflow — routing, plus prompt chaining across steps. ch. 4
